message.content: The question concerns discrete random variables. It asks about expectations of two variables. It also asks about the expectation of their sum. A finite expectation means the variable is integrable. For a discrete variable, integrability controls both positive and negative parts. If X is integrable, its positive part has finite expectation. If X is integrable, its negative part has finite expectation. The same condition holds for Y. Then the sum X plus Y is a random variable. The sum is finite almost surely if both variables are finite almost surely. Integrability is preserved under addition. The positive part of X plus Y is bounded by the positive parts of X and Y. The negative part of X plus Y is bounded by the negative parts of X and Y. These bounds use standard inequalities. No dependence assumption changes this conclusion. The result holds for any joint distribution. The result holds for independent variables. The result holds for dependent variables. Thus the expectation of the sum cannot be undefined. It also cannot be infinite. The expectation equals the sum of the expectations. The answer follows from basic measure theory. The short answer is no because whenever both discrete variables have finite expectations their sum is integrable and the expectation of that sum exists even if we carefully inspect the written mathematical details beneath the symbols.
